text:
Einstein didn't fail math. He mastered calculus by about 15 and got top marks in math and physics. The myth likely comes from a misread Swiss grading scale (6 was the top grade at his school) and from his failing the non-science sections of the ETH entrance exam at 16, two years early, while scoring exceptionally in math and physics. If your kid looks it up, the story will collapse and take your argument with it.

"Grades don't matter" is also not quite true, and kids notice. Grades affect course access, scholarships, and some admissions, so they matter somewhat. They don't measure intelligence, effort, or worth, and a bad grade is information about what to fix, not a verdict.

A more honest framing: "Grades measure how well you did on specific tasks at a specific time. They're useful feedback and they open some doors, but they don't define how smart you are or how your life goes. What matters more is whether you're learning and willing to improve."

If you want a true example of setbacks, use Edison's teachers' reports, which are also shaky, so better to pick documented ones: Einstein's rejection from ETH on the first try is real, and so is the fact that he was then rejected for teaching jobs after graduating and worked in a patent office.
